items.title: About the Wallabies
items.text:
Australia played its first Test in 1899, against a touring British Isles side at the Sydney Cricket Ground. The name Wallabies comes from the 1908 tour of Britain and has stayed with the men’s team ever since.

The Wallabies won the Rugby World Cup in 1991 and again in 1999, the first team to lift the trophy twice. They have played New Zealand for the Bledisloe Cup since 1932, and meet New Zealand, South Africa and Argentina every year in The Rugby Championship.

data.headline: 1991 and 1999: the two World Cup wins
data.standfirst: The Wallabies were the first team to win the Rugby World Cup twice. A look back at both titles.

image.alt: A gold trophy on a white background

body.text: Australia has won the men’s Rugby World Cup twice, in 1991 and 1999. At the time of the second win, no other country had lifted the trophy more than once.

image.alt: Rugby goal posts in a full stadium

body.caption: Twickenham, where Australia won its first title.

body.text: The 1991 tournament was played in Britain, Ireland and France. Australia met England in the final at Twickenham and won to become world champions for the first time.
Winning it once was a dream. Winning it twice made it a tradition.
Eight years later the final was in Cardiff, where Australia beat France to take the title again.
In 2027 the tournament comes to Australia, with the final in Sydney.

data.headline: The Wallabies: the story so far
data.standfirst: Australia played its first Test in 1899, against a touring British Isles side at the Sydney Cricket Ground. The name Wallabies comes from the 1908 tour of Britain and has stayed with the men’s team ever since.

image.alt: A rugby team celebrating together on the field

body.text: The Wallabies won the Rugby World Cup in 1991 and again in 1999, the first team to lift the trophy twice. They have played New Zealand for the Bledisloe Cup since 1932, and meet New Zealand, South Africa and Argentina every year in The Rugby Championship.
In 2027 the Rugby World Cup returns to Australia for the first time since 2003.
Players reach the Wallabies through club rugby, state teams and the national pathway. Every player who pulls on the jersey gets a cap number, counting every international since the first.

data.headline: A first-timer’s guide to a Test match
data.standfirst: Going to your first international? Here is how to make the most of the day.

image.alt: A lineout in a stadium with spectators in the stands

body.text: A Test match is the biggest day on the rugby calendar. Crowds are bigger than at club or Super Rugby games, so a little planning goes a long way.
Public transport is usually the easiest way to reach the stadium. Gates open about two hours before kick-off, and arriving early means you see the warm-ups and are in your seat for the anthems.
Wear the colours and bring a jacket for night games. Kids are welcome, and many stadiums have family areas.
Expect queues for transport after the final whistle. Staying for a drink or a bite while the crowd clears often makes for an easier trip home.
